summary.text: A probability distribution describes how probabilities are assigned to the possible results of a random phenomenon.
It is closely linked to random variables: a random variable assigns a value to each outcome and so induces a distribution on the values it can take.
Discrete distributions are described by probability mass functions, while many continuous distributions use probability density functions.

paragraphs.heading: How likely each result is
paragraphs.text: A probability distribution describes how probabilities are shared out among the possible results of something random. Put informally, it tells you how likely each result is. More exactly, the probabilities go to events, and an event is a set of possible outcomes of an experiment whose result is left to chance. The set of every possible outcome is called the sample space, often written Ω, and it can hold numbers, vectors, labels or anything else.

paragraphs.heading: Random variables
paragraphs.text: Distributions are closely tied to random variables. A random variable is a function that gives a value to every outcome of an experiment, and in doing so it produces a distribution over the values it can take. A coin toss, for instance, can be turned into a random variable X that is 1 for heads and 0 for tails. If the coin is fair, X = 1 and X = 0 are each given a probability of 1/2.

paragraphs.heading: Discrete distributions
paragraphs.text: Most distributions fall into one of two classes. A discrete distribution suits cases where the set of possible outcomes is discrete, such as a coin toss or a roll of a die. Its probabilities are given by a probability mass function, a rule that assigns a probability to each outcome. When a fair die is thrown, each face from 1 to 6 gets probability 1/6 of landing on top.

paragraphs.heading: Continuous distributions
paragraphs.text: An absolutely continuous distribution suits outcomes that can take any value in a continuous range, such as the temperature on a given day. Here the probabilities come from a probability density function, and the chance that the value lands in some interval is found by integrating that function over the interval. Only events made of infinitely many outcomes, like intervals, can have a probability above zero. The normal distribution is a common example of this kind.

paragraphs.heading: The ham on the scale
paragraphs.text: Imagine weighing a piece of ham on a supermarket scale that could show as many digits as you like. The chance that the ham weighs exactly 500 g has to be zero, since however precise the reading, you can never rule out more non-zero digits after the ones shown. Yet a rule such as a "500 g" pack having to weigh between 490 g and 510 g can be met. That works because a range does not ask the scale for infinite precision, and it leaves some room for natural variation.

paragraphs.heading: One variable or several
paragraphs.text: A distribution whose sample space is one-dimensional is called univariate; one whose sample space is a vector space of two or more dimensions is called multivariate. A univariate distribution gives the chances of a single random variable taking different values. A multivariate one, also called a joint distribution, covers a list of two or more random variables taking values together. Well-known univariate examples include the binomial, hypergeometric and normal distributions.
